observes that many posts are vacant in important Speciality Departments such as Anaesthesiology,
Anatomy, and General Medicine etc. Though 13 Super speciality Departments are functional in
AIIMS Patna but the large number of vacancy in each of these Departments is a grave concern
and raises serious question over the quality of healthcare.
5.49 In reply to a query about offering of incentives to the specialists and super specialists, AIIMS
Patna submitted that the decision needs to be taken by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
5.50 The Committee believes that Speciality and Super Speciality Departments are fundamental
for an Institute like AIIMS Patna that is envisaged as a flag bearer in providing tertiary
health care and medical education. The Committee however is anguished to note that
important Departments like Endocrinology, Nephrology, Urology, and Nuclear Medicine are
not functional till date in the Institute. Considering the fact that around 2.2 lakh new
patients suffering from End Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) are reported every year which
results in an additional demand of 3.4 crore dialysis every year, the status of crucial
Department like Nephrology being non-functional in AIIMS Patna is a matter of grave
concern.
5.51 The Institute needs to be considerate towards the expenses borne by poor patients
when they are referred to other hospitals because of non-availability of the medical facility
in AIIMS Patna. The Committee, thus, recommends to the Institute to start the Specialty
and Super Speciality Departments as early as possible in the best interest of the people of
the State.
5.52 The Committee recognises the fact that there is a dire need to address the shortage
of specialist and start the recruitment process for each Department. AIIMS Patna’s contention
that the decision for offering incentives to Specialists/Super Specialist will be taken by the
Ministry amounts to shirking off its responsibilities and therefore, the Committee strongly
recommends that the proposal of offering special incentives and packages to Specialist and
Super Specialists in AIIMS Patna be submitted to the Ministry for consideration without
much delay.
Medical Education
5.53 AIIMS Patna in its submission before the Committee stated that there are total 39 Departments
functional in AIIMS Patna, with 100 MBBS seats and 60 seats in nursing courses. Presently, the
Institute has MBBS and Nursing courses and is planning to start courses in para-medical, technician
etc. AIIMS Patna also provides facility of General Medicine Care, and super speciality treatment
for the people of Bihar. The average per day OPD and IPD footfall is 1775 and 49 respectively
(as per September, 2018).
5.54 The Committee was also informed that AIIMS Patna is actively involved in research activities
and post graduate courses with 78 students will start from January, 2019. Other Departments are
being evaluated by the External Experts from AIIMS, New Delhi and soon these Departments will
start PG/DM/M.ch process from July 2019 session. AIIMS Patna has 10 crores of extramural
funding in research and 28 extramural projects are being funded by agencies such as ICMR,
UNICEF, DBT, DST, WHO and Government of Bihar.

76
5.55 The Committee is unhappy to note the slow progress in starting Post Graduate courses
in different Departments of the Institute. The Institute should take cognizance of the acute
shortage of specialists in the country in general and in Bihar in particular and therefore
need to focus on producing better qualified specialists. The Committee, at the same time,
is aggrieved at the insufficient number of faculty staff in AIIMS Patna and worries that in
the absence of the required number of Professors/Additional Professor/Associate Professor/
Assistant Professor in the Institute, the quality of medical education may suffer. Therefore,
the Committee recommends that AIIMS Patna, before starting any Post graduate course in
the Institute, should ensure that the necessary infrastructure and human resource is available
with the Institute.
5.56 The Committee reprimands that AIIMS Patna does not have a human resource development
cell for undertaking regular induction and in service training programs for capacity building
of the staff. The Committee believes that training of personnel is critical for development
of high standards of medical education in AIIMS Patna. The Committee, therefore, strongly
recommends creation of a Human Resource Development Cell in AIIMS Patna that would
conduct regular training for the doctors, nurses and the staff. The Institute must also
conduct special training for ensuring palliative care to the patients.
5.57 As regards clinical training, AIIMS Patna stated that in the beginning of new session every
year, it conducts orientation programme and briefs the students about theory and clinical learning
details. There is one senior resident per 3 MBBS student. Approximately 20 students are posted per
ward as per clinical posting schedule. Clinical training is done as per each Departmental pre
specified standard and is imparted under faculty and senior residents.
5.58 The Committee is sceptical about the standard of clinical training provided as the
Institute has shortage of faculty in almost every Department. The Committee is anguished
to find that there are insufficient number of Operation Theatres and laboratories as the
construction work is yet to be completed. The Committee strongly emphasizes that the
assessment of the budding doctors should be based on real clinical cases rather than on
rote learning. Ideally, each hospital should have senior consultants to advise the resident
doctors on treatment or supervise the key procedure and surgeries but the shortage of
trained specialists in AIIMS Patna may produce graduates and post graduates with no
practical medical skills. Therefore, the Committee lays more impetus on imparting practical,
technical and skill based knowledge to the doctors. The Committee is of the view that
AIIMS Patna should, therefore, focus on producing better trained doctors who later become
competent enough to work in a clinical setting and possess sharp clinical and medical
acumen.

Theatres (OTs) have been sanctioned in AIIMS Patna but at present only 13 are functional, out
of which 11 are Modular Operation Theatres. As per information given by AIIMS Patna, 3174
major and minor surgeries and 506 emergency surgeries (including Caesarean), have been performed
till 25 November, 2018. The waiting time in surgical procedures varies from 1 week to 6 months

77
due to the limited availability of OTs at present. AIIMS Patna also informed that more OTs will

surgeries is reduced.

that AIIMS, Patna has conducted on an average 10 surgeries per day in its 13 Operation
Theatres. Moreover, only 506 emergency surgeries have been conducted. The Committee
finds that these 13 OTs remain highly underutilised although AIIMS Patna cited limited
availability of OTs as the reason behind the waiting time in surgical procedures. The Committee
also recommends to AIIMS, Patna for planning higher number of surgeries to be carried out
in a day so that one OT can be used for more than one surgery in a day, thus, resulting
in optimum utilisation of the Operation Theatre.
5.61 As per the information submitted by the Ministry, AIIMS Patna has conducted 4224
major and minor surgeries till September, 2018, the Committee is displeased with such huge
variation in the data and would like AIIMS Patna to submit precise data with respect to
surgical procedures (patient-wise and Department-wise) till date, since inception of the Institute,
within three months of presentation of this Report.

5.65 The Committee observes with deep concern that the numbers of beds in some important
Departments are very low. The low bed strength in each Department also reflects the

should also ensure that the timeline for completion of Burns and Plastic surgery Department

5.69 AIIMS Patna submitted that there is no waiting time for investigation of cases (X ray,

within 24 hours. For OPD cases, the average waiting period for X ray is 1 day to 3 days, for

waiting period 1 month. For MRI OPD cases the waiting period is 8 Months. AIIMS Patna cited
shortage of MRI machines as the reason for long waiting period and insisted on procurement of
two more MRI machines. AIIMS Patna also submitted that on an average 5 MRIs, 2 X-ray
mammography and 8-10 Sono-mammography are conducted per working day.
5.70 The Committee is shocked at the long waiting period for Ultrasound, CT scan, and
MRI OPD Cases. The Committee during its study visit to Patna also came across patients
with waiting period as long as one year. The medical imaging facilities are fundamental for
the correct diagnosis of any disease but such long waiting period render the whole medical
care process futile and life threatening. The Committee is not at all convinced by the plea
of AIIMS Patna’s management that shortage of MRI machines led to such long waiting
period for MRI scans. The Committee also notes that AIIMS Patna on an average conducted
only 5 MRI per day, 2 Mammography and 18 CT scan which is very low when compared to
the available infrastructure and manpower. The Committee believes that even with one MRI
machine at its disposal, the Institute could have easily carried out more than twenty scans
in one day as is being done in other AIIMS and private hospitals. The grim data furnished
by AIIMS Patna clearly reflects gross underutilization of the available resources and sheds
light on the failure of the institute to work in its full capacity. The Committee during its
earlier study visit observed that RIMS Imphal conducted 30 MRI scans per day on a very
old machine and also carried out over 50 CT scans. The Committee desires a quarterly
update from AIIMS Patna on the per day usage of MRI machine along with the daily
pending cases.  The Committee strongly recommends that the procurement of second MRI
machine should only be done when the present MRI machine is optimally utilised.

professionals, AYUSH through its traditional methods of treatment can go a long way in

Monitoring Mechanism
5.77 The Committee is of the considered view that the success of any project lies in
effective implementation and evaluation. State Project Monitoring Committee (State PMC)
were entrusted with the responsibility to monitor the progress of new AIIMS in the State.
This Committee was required to meet at least once in a quarter to review the progress of
AIIMS. In the State of Bihar no such State project Monitoring Committee (State PMC) has
been constituted and in the absence of the required mechanism, no meetings could be
conducted. The Committee feels that the various issues plaguing AIIMS Patna could have
been easily solved had the concept of State PMC was implemented on ground.
5.78 AIIMS Patna, an Institute of National Importance today trails behind in many areas
that are fundamental for providing quality healthcare. The Committee expects AIIMS Patna
to make extra efforts to build itself into a world class institute as envisioned while establishing
the institute.

Institute in execution of the project. The changes in the design at such a later stage would
have a negative impact on the expansion program, in terms of additional resources, cost and
extended project duration. It seems to the Committee that obviously the Institute had not
conducted any proper study before planning the expansion of phase-II residential complex.
The preparation of revised drawing, revised detailed estimates and tender documents would
require additional time resulting in cost and time overruns. The Committee, therefore,
underlines the need for proper planning and evaluation by engaging reputed agencies before
undertaking any construction projects.
Status of Faculty and Non Faculty Strength
6.17 It has been informed to the Committee that only 125 faculty posts have been filled up out
of total sanctioned strength of 305 and 180 faculty posts are still lying vacant. As per data
submitted by the Ministry, out of the total 3776 sanctioned non-faculty strength, only 1453 posts
are filled up whereas 2323 are vacant.
6.18 The Committee learnt that only 11 Professors are presently working out of 54 sanctioned

87
posts and 43 posts are lying vacant. The Institute has been able to fill up 33 posts of Additional
Professors out of 45 sanctioned posts, 53 posts of Associate Professors against 81 sanctioned
posts and 51 posts of Assistant Professor out of 125 sanctioned posts.
6.19 The Committee has been reiterating that shortage of qualified medical professional is
one of the key challenges that new AIIMS are presently facing. The Committee notes that
huge number of posts in both faculty and non faculty posts are lying vacant at AIIMS, Raipur.
Out of total sanctioned posts of 4089, 2636 posts are lying vacant that constitutes more than
64 per cent of the total sanctioned posts. The Committee, further, observes that majority of
the vacancies are at the Professor/Additional Professor level which indicates that the Institute
is suffering from dearth of experienced personnel. The Committee believes that health care
is one of the most labour-intensive sectors where human resources are crucial. Merely developing
infrastructure and increasing capital expenditure would not help, instead it is adequate manpower
at the health care Institutes that ensures efficient and prompt delivery of health care services
to the patients.  The Committee, therefore, would like the Institute to make concerted efforts
and accord equal priority to fill up the vacant posts.
6.20 The Institute needs to engage itself with continuous assessment of the gap in demand
and supply of human resources and take suitable steps/measures to fill up the gap. The
Committee is of the view that career aspiration, socio-economic status, organizational policies,
work environment, growth opportunities, infrastructural facilities are the main factors that
influence the decision of any health personnel to join any health care Institute. The Committee,
therefore, recommends to the Institute to focus on strengthening these crucial parameters
to attract adequate number of health care personnel.
6.21 The Committee is perturbed to observe that majority of the non faculty posts are
engaged either on contract or have been outsourced. The Committee believes that such
adhoc arrangements for deployment of medical professionals on contractual basis results in
disturbing issues of inconsistency in carrying on daily task that ultimately affects the
overall functioning of the Institute. It also affects the motivational level of the staff due
to prevailing uncertainties about job security and stability and thereby, lack of sense of
belongingness towards the organization.  Hence, the Committee calls upon the Institute to
strive for employing staff on permanent basis for ensuring continued and better delivery of
services.

6.23 The Committee finds that the status of vacancies in 18 Specialty and 12 Super Specialty
Departments is equally appalling. Under Specialty Departments,   out of a total of 146

Surgical Gastroenterology, Nephrology, Medical Oncology/Hematology, Surgical Oncology and
Gastroenterology are not functional at AIIMS, Raipur. The Committee believes that there are
many diseases which require specialty diagnosis and treatment necessitating the availability
of Specialty and Super Specialty Departments. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the
Institute to make these Departments functional without any delay so that tertiary healthcare
services is made available for the patients from Chhattisgarh and neighbouring States.
Procurement of Equipment
6.25 The Committee has been informed that AIIMS, Raipur has implemented Central Public Procurement
Portal since 08-03-2017 and 100% tender cases are being uploaded in this portal. The use of
Central Public Procurement Portal not only provides wide publicity, but also helps in ensuring
competition and better rates. The Institute is also using GeM (Government e-market place) for
procurement of various items/equipment for its use.
6.26 The CAG in its 10th report has pointed out delay of 3 to 23 months in supply of 58 items
of equipment including ICU ventilator, CT 128 slice, orthopaedic operation theatre and MRI machine
valuing ` 44.46 crore in AIIMS Raipur.  42 equipment costing ` 33.80 crore were installed with
delay ranging from 4 to 41 months.  Further, 76 equipment costing ` 3.85 crore procured during
1      2 3 4 5 6

90
July, 2013 to December, 2016  were either not functional or remained unutilized/underutilised. The
reasons for equipment being non-functional were poor after sales service, equipment being defective
at the time of installation, breakdowns and absence of required manpower for operating the equipment.
6.27 The Committee deprecates the Institute for poor management of crucial equipment
worth crores. Procurement process involves commissioning, installation, training, warranty,
after sales services like post-warranty maintenance and assured availability of spares.  The
Committee is of the view that delay in the installation of procured equipment may jeopardize
after sales services for warranty period may lapse as per the contract. The Committee would
like the Institute to install the equipment as soon as these equipment are delivered. Further,
the equipment must be purchased only when the suitable infrastructure and manpower for
their installation and operation is available.
6.28 The Committee feels that delay in the delivery or installation of the equipment at the
Institute is certainly not a healthy trend. It deprives patients of diagnostic/therapeutic
benefits through the usage of such equipment. The delay in the supply of the equipment
is the fault on the part of the PSA/supplier/manufacturer and the Institute must take
suitable action against the errant supplier. The Committee is of the view that procurement
of equipment is a key area and therefore the Institute must resolve these issues by making
the PSA accountable for any delay and lapse.
6.29 The Committee is of the further view that quality of medical equipment needs to be
looked into because defective equipment result in frequent break-down of healthcare services.
Given the importance of medical equipment in diagnosis as well as treatment and the high
price involved in purchase of several hi-tech equipment, it is imperative that the equipment
are put to their best use for optimum utilization of resources. Non-installation of equipment
is indicative of lackadaisical approach of the Institute in letting them remain idle which is
mere wastage of resources at the cost of taxpayers’ money. The Committee, accordingly,
recommends the Institute to take strict action against the manufacturers for delayed delivery
or delivery of defective equipment. The Committee, further, recommends that Institute
should either exchange the defective equipment with new equipment or scrap the contract
with the manufacturers by seeking adequate legal redressal. The Committee recommends
for an action taken status report on the specific observations of the CAG in context of
procurement of medical equipment and recommends the Ministry to take strict action against
the errant officials.
6.30 In a specific query regarding the total number of medical equipment and procured with USFDA
certification and those with any other certification that have been procured at the Institute, the
Committee has been informed that in last two years, 159 types of medical equipment have been
procured with USFDA certification and 52 types of equipment have been procured with other certification.
6.31 The Committee observes that majority of 159 types of medical equipment during the
last two years have been purchased with USFDA certification. The Committee is concerned
at the substantial number of procurement done in AIIMS, Raipur with USFDA certification.
The Committee apprehends that some of them may be available with European/Indian
manufacturers. The Committee, in this connection, reiterates its recommendation made on

91
other AIIMS that the Institute must give preference to general CE/BIS certification to
increase competitive bidding. The Committee feels that where the equipment with BIS
certification is available, the Indian manufacturers should be given priority over the USFDA
or other certifications. The Institute should make efforts to contribute to the “Make in
India”, scheme of Government of India to give boost to Indian manufacturers. Further,
USFDA certification involves higher cost of equipment which would unfortunately be passed
on to the patients seeking treatment and care and thereby increasing their out of pocket
expenditure. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that USFDA certification may
be resorted to only in exceptional circumstances where other manufacturers do not match
the high parameters or urgency of equipment with higher standard is called for. The Committee
desires that the Institute should submit a status report on all medical devices/equipment
procured with USFDA certification/single bid/proprietary certification alongwith reasons for
doing so, within three months of presentation of this report to the Parliament.
6.32 The Committee hopes that AIIMS Raipur is adhering to procedure of multiple tendering
in the purchase of medical equipment and avoiding single bid purchase to ensure transparency
and public trust in procurement system of medical equipment.
Medical Education
6.33 AIIMS, Raipur started its academic journey in the September, 2012 with the first batch of
50 students joining the MBBS programme. From the year 2013, each batch has 100 students joining
the MBBS course. The College of Nursing started functioning in 2013 with intake of 60 students
each year. The Institute has started Post Graduate from July, 2013 in 22 Departments. A Post
graduate course have also commenced in the College of Nursing from July, 2018.
6.34 The Committee was given to understand that out of the 30 total PG seats, only 22
seats were filled in July, 2018. The seats in six Departments i.e. Anatomy, Biochemistry,
Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, Microbiology, Pharmacology and Physiology remained vacant.
The Committee expects the Institute to assess the reasons for the vacant seats and take
remedial action so that all seats get filled up from the next session onwards.
6.35 The Ministry has informed the Committee that clinical training is imparted MBBS students
from third semester onwards upto the ninth semester and also during one year compulsory
rotatory internship programme. For nursing students, the clinical training is imparted from first
year onwards upto the fourth year. For postgraduate students of clinical Departments, the entire
three years period is devoted to clinical training while for students of non-clinical and para-clinical
Departments, relevant clinical training is imparted as per the approved curriculum. Undergraduate
students have been imparted hands-on clinical training by faculty members and senior residents.
Adequate numbers of faculty members are available in the Institute for providing clinical training
to undergraduate students. The ratio of number of undergraduate students per Senior Resident in
a ward is approximately 20:1.
6.36 The Committee feels that clinical training is a vital part in a medical education for
becoming a successful doctor. The Committee is, however, apprehensive about the quality of
the clinical training imparted at the Institute to the undergraduate and postgraduate students
due to shortage of faculty at the Institute as many key Departments are being handled by

92
a single faculty. The Committee wonders how an Institute is accomplishing the objective of
imparting clinical training to the medical students with limited number of faculty. The
Committee also notes that seats under many PG courses are lying vacant which raises a
question mark about the quality of clinical training facilities available at the Institute.
Poor clinical training hampers the professional pursuit of doctors which amounts to risking
the lives of the patients. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Institute to ensure
adequate faculty at the Institute for imparting quality medical education and clinical training
to the students aspiring to be well-trained doctors.
Status of Operation Theatre (OTs) and Intensive Care Unit (ICUs)
6.37 The Committee has been informed that 28 Modular Operation Theaters (MOTs) have been
sanctioned for the Institute. Presently, 8 MOTs are functioning with state-of-the-art equipment and
fully functional medical gas pipeline system. Commissioning of remaining 20 MOTs is under
progress. Remaining MOTs will be completed by December, 2018.
6.38 The Committee is of the view it is unfortunate that even after a lapse of considerable
period of time, only 8 operation theatres have been made functional. AIIMS, Raipur was
established with the aim of providing economical and reliable healthcare services to the
people visiting the hospital. Thus, the limited availability of OTs will definitely have an
adverse effect on the services provided by the Institute. The Committee hopes that the
Institute will expedite the process of construction of the remaining OTs to ensure that all
OTs are made functional without procrastination.
6.39 The Committee has not been able to assess the number of surgical procedures carried
out in AIIMS Raipur due to the variation in the data furnished by the Institute and the
Ministry. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that precise data with respect to
major and minor surgeries done (patient-wise and Department-wise) till date since the
inception of the Institute, may be submitted to the Committee within three months of
presentation of this Report.
6.40 On  a query related to  status of  ICUs at AIIMS, Raipur, the Committee was  informed that
there are four ICUs namely surgical ICU with 7 beds, Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) with
6 beds, Paediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) with 8 Beds and High Dependency Unit (HDU) with
5 beds. All the beds in these ICUs are equipped with ventilators, monitors, syringe pumps and
defibrillators. Out of 100 sanctioned beds, only 26 are functional. A total of 35 ventilators are
available in the hospital. The ICU facility in different clinical Departments requires high-end critical
care by fully trained personnel.
6.41 The Committee notes with concern that only 26 beds out of total sanctioned strength
of 100 beds are functional at the Institute. ICUs are used to provide specialized rehabilitative
care to patients as they start to recover from their critical illness or injury. The Committee
believes that bed scarcity in ICU may result in refusal of admission to initial patients,
thereby, depriving them the benefit of ICU services. The Committee observes that there are
as many as 35 ventilators for 26 ICU beds, indicating that 9 ventilators are lying unused
in the ICUs. The Committee feels that the value of the equipment starts depreciating
immediately after they are procured and non-functioning of the equipment results in loss

93
of their value. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Institute to increase the
number of beds so that critically ill patients are not refused the service of ICUs due to
scarcity of beds and focus on optimum utilization of resources available.
Dialysis Facilities
6.42 The Committee has been informed that there is no faculty member in the Nephrology Department.
Earlier one faculty member had joined but resigned after six months. The dialysis facility will start
only after faculty member in Nephrology Department are appointed. The Institute is actively pursuing
faculty selections in various Super-Specialty Departments including Nephrology.
6.43 The Committee believes that Nephrology Department constitutes an important part of
any health institution in providing Super Specialty health care services to the patients.
Absence of the faculty would mean that patients requiring dialysis or treatment related to
renal diseases would be turned away due to non-functioning of the Department. The Committee,
therefore, recommends to the Institute to recruit the faculty as early as possible so that
dialysis services become functional at the Institute without any delay.
Ayush
6.44 The Committee was informed that AIIMS, Raipur started the AYUSH services in the year
2014. Till 2015, Homoeopathy and Ayurveda services were available at the Institute. In the year
2017-18, the Institute treated 4078 OPD patients, it is however, not providing IPD services in
AYUSH.
6.45 The sanctioned strength for Senior Medical Officer AYUSH and Yoga Instructor is one each
in the Institute and sanctioned strength for Medical Officer AYUSH is 5. At present one Senior
Medical Officer in the field of Ayurveda is working in AIIMS Raipur for the last four years and
serving patients in Ayurveda OPD. One Medical Officer (Homeopathy) was also working from
28.08.2014 to 28.12.2015. The doctor to patient ratio is 1:30 (approximately) for OPD.
6.46 The Committee observes that out of 5 AYUSH services, only Ayurveda services are
functional at the Institute at the present. The Committee underlines the need for starting
other branches of AYUSH system at the Institute so that the patients avail the facilities and
services of an alternate system of medicine. Patients would be benefitted immensely as
AYUSH medicines are not only cost effective but also widely used as a standalone option or
as adjunct with bio medicine in the diseases entailing long duration of treatment. The
Committee feels that the relevance of AYUSH has become more prominent due to this
paradigm shift in the health sector. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Institute
to start other Ayush services as well as IPD services at the Institute without any further
delay.
6.47 The Committee notes that out of 7 sanctioned posts, only one post has been filled up
yet. One Senior Medical Officer (Ayurveda) is working on contractual basis since 1st September
2014. The Committee believes that the Institute needs to strengthen its in AYUSH wing and
provide cost effective and equitable AYUSH health care services throughout the country by
improving access to the services as envisaged under National Ayush Mission. To ensure the
optimal development and propagation of AYUSH systems of health care, there is the need

94
to have adequate faculty in the AYUSH Department of the Institute. The Committee, thus,
recommends to the Institute to fill up the vacant posts in the AYUSH Department on
regular basis without further delay.
6.48 The Committee finds AIIMS, Raipur to be lacking behind on almost all parameters.
However, the Committee would be taking AIIMS, Raipur for detailed examination and will
conduct a study visit which could not be done this time due to time constraints.

vacancies in engineering positions in the Project Cell of the new AIIMS and abandonment
of works by Project Consultants and delay in making alternate arrangements. These reasons
were indicative of deficient project and contract management, administrative laxity and weak
monitoring. It was incumbent upon the departments to take effective steps where necessary to
mitigate the delays, remove bottlenecks and expedite the progress.”
7.14 The Committee is of the view that underutilisation of the funds during years 2011-2017
is the main reason behind the delay in completion of the project and cost overruns. The
Committee expresses its concern over delay and cost overruns in different projects of
various packages. Time and cost over runs are undesirable in projects under construction.
The delays in construction project have delayed delivery of health services. The Committee
observes that delay in completion of the project was on account of poor planning, unrealistic
scheduling of the dates, lack of communication between the contracting agency and the
authorities concerned at the Institute and poor monitoring.
7.15 The delay in the completion of the project has also been attributed to services by
former Project Consultant. The Committee believes that the track record of delivery of
projects of the contractor as well as Project Consultant must be taken into account before
awarding such important project work to them. The Committee, therefore, recommends the

100
Ministry to examine the reasons for delay in the construction projects and fix responsibility
and accountability for delayed work in all four packages. The Committee further recommends
to the Ministry/Institute to engage other professional agencies or other reputed construction
majors for upcoming new AIIMS to ensure cost effective and timely execution of projects
especially in projects where implementing agencies have failed to ensure timely completion.
7.16 W ith regard to residential complex, the Committee has been informed that the residential
project as per the contract has been completed by M/s HSCC (I) Ltd. but it is not as per staff
strength. The work for residential complex was started on 18th September, 2008 and original date
of completion was 3rd March, 2016 but the work actually got completed on 26th September, 2017.
The Committee has been informed that the Institute is having sufficient number of hostel accommodation
for the present strength of students. The demand for residential accommodation from the faculty
and non-faculty is minimal as private accommodation is available in the adjoining area. However,
action is being taken to construct new accommodation for senior residents, nursing and para-medical
staff in the second phase. The Committee has been informed that there is more requirement of the
physical layout/infrastructure of the Institute to accommodate all Departments/teaching faculties.
7.17 The Committee is happy to note that management of AIIMS Bhubaneswar has explored
the idea of private residential accommodation in the adjoining areas. The Committee understands
that new AIIMS, still facing infrastructure constraints can easily avoid undue stress through
arrangement of private accommodation in the nearby areas and the limited resource can
better be utilized on creation of much needed physical infrastructure. The Committee
acknowledges AIIMS Bhubaneswar for its sound judgment and right emphasis on the more
important requirements and demands of the Institute. The Committee also appreciates the
Institute for completing all the construction projects under the four Packages. The Committee
recommends the Institute to expedite and monitor the other construction activities and
work on creating the required infrastructure for accommodating all its Departments.

Procurement of Medical Equipment
7.20 AIIMS, Bhubaneswar has shared the following status of procurement of equipment in AIIMS,
Bhubaneswar:-
(a) All the equipment worth above `2.50 lakh are being procured by AIIMS, Bhubaneswar
through e-tender/tender. The number of bidders in e-tender/tender are very few and in
technical evaluation of the bids, sometimes all the bidders get disqualified due to not
fulfillment of technical requirements. Retendering process with revised specification is
quite time consuming as well.
(b) Sometimes, after due technical evaluation, it is found that only one bidder is qualifying
in the e-tender/tender. Taking into urgency of patient care and certificate from the
indenter, the Institute has to finalize some cases in single bid after following the relevant
provision of GFR.
(c) The e-tender/tender terms and conditions are made as per the instructions of the
MoHFW which provides that there should be 5 years warranty and 5 years CMC after
completion of warranty period. The same perhaps is seen as a bottleneck to get
responses from more bidders and it also makes the price quoted by bidder at higher
side.
(d) The Institute presently finalizes the technical specification of equipment costing more
than `30 lakh with the involvement of the DGHS nominee as per the extant instructions
of the Ministry. This process takes a lot of time due to non-availability of DGHS
nominee in time for finalizing the technical specification. As a result, the procurement
process gets delayed. In this regard, it is suggested that broad based technical specifications
for equipment may be finalized either by technical expert for all the AIIMS regarding
procurement of high end/sophisticated equipment for all AIIMSs or technical specification
of the AIIMS, New Delhi for similar equipment may be followed.
(e) Sometimes it is felt that after finalisation of the tendering process, some of the bidders
are back-tracking to execute the order due to high fluctuation in value of foreign
currency.
7.21 The Committee takes cognizance of the problems highlighted by the Institute in the
procurement of the equipment. The Committee observes that sometimes even after multiple
floating of tender, only single bid is received and there are few cases when multiple bids

102
are received but only single bid gets qualified on technical grounds. The Committee believes
that there is a need to advertise the tender to be floated on a large scale so that more and
more manufacturers submit their bids leading to competitive pricing and availability of
many options for procurement of equipment. The Committee, thus, recommends to the
Institute to advertise their tenders in the national dailies and also integrate into the system
of the Central Public Procurement Portal for wider dissemination of information regarding
the floating of tender so as to make it accessible to large number of manufacturers. The
Committee, further, recommends to the Institute to list out the technical requirements
more clearly by making them generic so that there are fewer chances of bids getting
disqualified on technical grounds. The tendency to deliberately design specifications to ensure
that procurement is done on proprietary/single bid basis should be avoided under all
circumstances.  The Committee would like to highlight that the problem areas as identified
by AIIMS, Bhubaneswar are welcome since it would help the procedural hurdles and help
in overall streamlining of the whole process of procurement of medical equipment. The idea
of finalizing uniform technical specification for requirement especially high end equipment
is certainly a step in the right direction.  The Committee strongly supports and recommends
for appropriate time bound action on the suggestions of AIIMS, Bhubaneswar for improving
the procurement process.

Tender wizard of M/S-ITI Ltd. for e-tendering similar to Central Public Procurement Portal. The

CHAPTER-VIII
UPGRADATION OF GOVERNMENT MEDICAL COLLEGES/
INSTITUTIONS UNDER PMSSY
8.1 Upgradation of several existing Government Medical Colleges/Institutions in different States of
the country is one of the two components under the PMSSY . The programme for upgradation of
Government Medical Colleges/Institutions (GMCIs) broadly includes the following (i) construction
of Super Specialty Blocks/Trauma Centers, (ii) procurement of medical equipment; (iii) generation
of employment opportunities; and (iv) enhancement of number of seats of Post Graduate and
Graduate courses in GMCs under PMSSY .
8.2 Post-Graduate seats and additional faculty posts as per norms will be created and filled up
in these GMCs by the respective State /UT Governments. The responsibility of running the new
facilities rests with the State Government which has to make all provisions, including complete
Human Resource (Specialist/ Super-specialists and paramedics etc). The Government decided to
increase the number the GMCs to be upgraded in subsequent phases of the scheme. After a review
of the coverage area of existing Government institutions and planned institutions and on the
recommendations of the Working Group for Tertiary Care Institutions for 12th Five Year Plan.
8.3 As per the information submitted by the Ministry, as of October 2018, 73 GMCs has been
approved for upgradation under the six-phases of PMSSY . A Total of 19 GMCs upgradation
projects were sanctioned in Phase I and II of the PMSSY , out of which 15 projects have been
completed. Upgradation of GMCs undertaken in Phase III and Phases-IV & V A are yet not complete
and construction activities at these Institutes are in progress.
8.4 The Ministry further informed the Committee that for the Phase-III and later phases upgradation
projects, Ministry in consultation with the State Governments has also focused on augmentation of
the PG seats in the process of creation of the Super-specialty infrastructure. Under the gap analysis
process, agreement of the State Government has also been taken for creation of the PG seats
which would become feasible with the operationalization of the new facilities.

for other purposes. For example, funds for procurement were diverted to meet cost escalation of
civil works and installation of gas manifold system, comprehensive maintenance contract and
purchase of consumables items. It was also observed that funds for computerization were diverted
for centralized air conditioning and minor civil works. The cases relate to GMCs which were
within the jurisdiction of the Institutes and State Governments. The CAG report further highlights
that in five GMCIs, funds amounting to ` 63.85 crore, received for civil works and procurement
of equipment, remained idle for periods ranging from two to five years.
8.10 The Committee takes into account the budgetary allocation and funding pattern  of
select 73 GMCs under five phases in PMSSY for which the Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare has released a total amount of `````5239.71 crore.  However, the State share is pending
in about 50% case of GMCs for upgradation works under Phase III. The Committee observes
that delay in release of State share has impacted the upgradation projects adversely. The
Committee desires the Ministry to urgently take the matter with State Governments concerned
to release their share at the earliest so that the work of GMCs does not suffer. The
Committee, in this regard, would like to emphasize that the Ministry/State Governments
concerned must comply with the fund sharing commitment to maintain the sanctity of

112
project. The Ministry needs to put in place a mechanism for release of funds within a
stipulated time period from both Centre and State Governments. The Committee, therefore,
recommends concerted action on part of both the Centre and State Governments to make
the upgradation project successful. The Committee, therefore, recommends that all out
efforts need to be taken by the Ministry to get all the procedural formalities/ necessary
approvals done well in time and the State Governments concerned need to be persuaded and
advised regularly in this regard. A quarterly status report on the pending position with
respect to the State share may also be provided to enable the Committee to take up the
matter with the concerned State Government as most of the delays are due to internal
processes of the States.
8.11 The Committee is of the view that the funds allocated to the project should be effectively
and efficiently utilized and not remain idle or underutilised as that would otherwise adversely
impact the smooth execution of the project. Moreover, such instances reflect faulty planning
and improper administration with regard to utilization of the allocated funds. The Committee
views this as a matter of concern. The Committee observes that upgradation of GMCs is
under the direct supervision of the Central Government, therefore, under utilization of the
allocated funds should not become a routine affair as the same would lead to further delays
in completion of projects causing time and cost overruns. The Committee, therefore, strongly
recommends that the Ministry must act promptly and monitor the effective and timely
utilization of funds.
8.12 The Committee views diversion of funds as criminal misappropriation of allocated fund
and violation of fiscal discipline. Such trend not only results in the shortfall of the funds
for completion of construction activities but is against the provisions of the MoU signed
between the Ministry and the States. Effective monitoring and accountability need to be
ensured so that funds released are utilised for the intended purpose. The Committee expects
the Ministry to issue strict advisories against the diversion of funds and fixing of responsibility
on GMCs/State Governments for the same.
Key Concern Areas
8.13 In reply to a specific query about the areas of concern/challenges in upgradation of GMCs,
the Ministry has submitted the following:-
(i) Timely availability of encumbrance free site in the GMCs has been one of the key
challenges faced in several projects under Phase III.  In many projects, the State
Governments have taken long time in making available encumbrance free sites.  There
have been delays in removal of pre-existing physical structures, services and, in some
cases, trees standing on the site by the respective State Governments.
(ii) Delays in deciding on the scope of the upgradation project in terms of the physical
facilities, number of beds, list of medical equipment etc.  by the GMCs/State  Governments
has been another concern.  Most of the States have found it difficult to firm up the
scope under the gap analysis, as, generally as per the perception of the States, the
requirements are much more than what the limited budget can accommodate.
(iii) There have also been instances of delay in the release of the State share. However, all

113
the States have given commitment to provide the State share. MoU with the State
Governments also have specific provision regarding the commitment of the State
Governments for the State share.  The delay in the release of the State share has
basically been due to the internal approval processes in the States. The issue has been
taken up at senior level in the State Governments through letters and over phone and
the State s have also been taking action for early release of the share.
8.14 The Ministry has taken up the various issues, with the State Governments and has flagged
in the Ministerial level interactions with the States at the level of Health and Family Welfare Minister
and MoS.  However, the progress of the projects has not been allowed to be suffered due to this
delay as the Ministry has ensured timely release of the central share to the Executive agencies
(EAs) and to the Procurement Support Agent (PSA).
CAG’s Observation
8.15 CAG Report highlighted many areas of concern in upgradation of GMCs which are as
follows:-
(i) Delay in commencement of projects in all three phases.
(ii) Inordinate delays in completion of construction works of GMCs after around of work
in the first three phases of PMSSY .
(iii) Non-compliance with codal and contract provisions as evident in Bangalore Medical
College and Research Institute (BMCRI), Bangalore, institute of medical science (IMS),
Varanasi, B.J. Medical College (BJMC), Ahmedabad, Gajra Raja Medical College (GRMC),
Gwalior.
(iv) Award of works at higher cost.
(v) Non-availability of equipment due to placement of orders, change in model of the
equipment and lack of follow up by the Institute.
(vi) Non-installation/delay in installment of equipment and idle/non-functional equipment.
(vii) Shortage of human resources in upgraded GMCs.
(viii) Non-functioning of super specialty facilities due to shortage of staff and due to lack of
equipment
8.16 The Committee takes note of the key concern areas of GMCs upgradation. The Committee
observes that the Ministry has put the entire onus on the State Governments for successful
implementation of the scheme. The Committee is of the view that the Central Government
has a key role in planning, guiding and monitoring the scheme. The Ministry needs to
consider State Governments as its partner in resolving the constraints being encountered in
administration of projects and sort out practical difficulties faced in implementation thereof.
There is a need for an efficacious monitoring mechanism to avoid inordinate delays in
completion of upgradation projects. The Committee, thus, recommends to the Ministry to
make a realistic assessment of the challenges faced and formulate suitable plan of action
in active coordination with the State Governments to overcome the same. All out efforts

114
must be made by both the Central Government and the State Governments to strive towards
completion of upgradation of GMCs within specified the timeline.
8.17 The attention of the Committee has been drawn to the CAG findings wherein serious
areas of concern have been highlighted especially w.r.t non-compliance of codal and contract
provision and awards of work at higher cost. The Committee is of the firm view that strict
compliance with codal and contract provision need to be adhered in all circumstances and
award of work should be assigned on merit and proven track record.
Selection of the GMCs for upgradation
8.18 In a specific query regarding the selection of GMCs for upgradation, the Committee has been
informed that  the Ministry, while finalizing the upgradation projects has given higher priority to the
States generally considered “backward” with respect to the broad socio-economic indicators. However,
the State has to also bear the State share and also operate and maintain the facilities created;
therefore, the willingness of the State to contribute its share and participate in the scheme is also
important apart from backwardness. As per the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) notes available
with the Ministry, all projects have been selected on the basis of demands raised by States and
therefore the States were fully involved in the selection process.
8.19 The Committee takes note that the recent CAG Report No. 10 of 2018 shows a different
picture altogether that the Ministry had not formulated any criteria or procedure for selection of
GMCs for upgradation as brought out below:–
I. In Bihar, two GMCs were selected for upgradation under PMSSY Phase-III by the
Ministry without consulting the Government of Bihar;
II. Three GMCs in Madhya Pradesh were approved for upgradation in Phase-III without
obtaining any preliminary project report from the State Government;
III. In Maharashtra, selection of six GMCs was done based on proposals submitted by their
respective Deans and not on the basis of any State level study;
IV . In Rajasthan, no record was available with the State Authorities of any request/proposal
for upgradation of GMCs under PMSSY; and
V . Ministry selected B.J. Medical College, Ahmedabad and Pandit Deendayal Upadhyay
Government Medical College, Rajkot for upgradation under the scheme in first and third
phase respectively without any proposal from the Government of Gujarat.
8.20 Attention of the Committee is drawn to the CAG report which further highlighted that there
is arbitrary selection and distribution of work amongst consultancy agencies. The Project Monitoring
Committee (PMC) in May, 2006 decided that for upgradation of GMCs, there was no need to
appoint separate Project Consultant for each Institute for upgradation of GMCs. It was instead
decided to engage CPWD, M/s HSCC or any other PSU already engaged in the Health sector as
consultant to assist the Ministry in effective implementation of the upgradation projects. Accordingly,
upgradation projects were allotted to the CPWD, M/s HSCC and M/s HLL/(M/s HITES) Ltd.
8.21 The CAG report further mentions that the distribution of GMCs among the three identified
agencies was done on nomination basis without any identifiable criteria for allocation of work.

115
Phase-I projects were allotted to CPWD and all GMCs in the Southern region were allotted to
M/s HLL without any detailed assessment of their capacities for undertaking works assigned to
them. In Phase-II, four out of six GMCs were allotted to M/s HLL only on the basis of direction
of the Minister in Charge and remaining two GMCs were allotted to M/s HSCC where no reasons
were available on record for allotting the work of Dr. Rajendra Prasad Government Medical College
(RPGMC), Tanda to the company. In the case of Phase-III projects, allocations were made on the
recommendations of a Technical Committee which met and made recommendations for allocation
on the basis of past performance on the same day that it was formed i.e. on 14 February, 2014.
However, the assessment of the past performance of the three agencies was not on record. The
works entrusted to these agencies in Phase-I and II suffered delays ranging from three months to
seven years, none of the works of Phase-III had been completed. The Ministry, in February, 2018
stated that there were no delays in works executed through M/s HSCC and M/s HLL. It added that
there was no need to evaluate performances for each phase as the PSUs were always under the
scrutiny in the Ministry. The reply of the Ministry is not acceptable as there is no record of any
assessment of the capabilities of the agencies before allocation of the work. Further, the fact that
all the GMCs entrusted to these agencies had faced significant delays in implementation undermines
Ministry’s claim of proper assessment of the capabilities of the agencies while allocating the work.
8.22 The CAG report highlighted that the Ministry had given an undertaking to the Planning
Commission at the scheme appraisal stage that it would sign a MoU with State Governments for
the running of the upgraded GMCIs and for ensuring that funds were being utilized. A commitment
was to be obtained from the State Governments for providing staff as per Medical Council of India
requirements and for taking up regular maintenance of the upgraded facilities. However, the Ministry
did not enter into any MoU with the State Governments concerned in respect of the GMCIs
upgraded during Phase-I and Phase-II. In the absence of such a MoU, in several cases, State
Governments did not provide required manpower for operation and maintenance of the upgraded
facilities.
8.23 The Committee feels that the Ministry has not devised scientific criteria/parameters
for the selection of GMCs under PMSSY. The Committee feels that the criteria of socio-
economic indicators, mainly the presence of already existing tertiary healthcare facilities,
should also be taken into account. The Committee also take into cognizance that  many
GMCs have been selected without consulting the respective States and even without considering
their financial condition and even without entering into any MoU with the State Governments.
Further, the selection of the consultancy agencies was purely arbitrary and no past record
of the agencies has been taken into consideration.  To consider HLL/HSCC as a panacea for
all execution is a area of serious concern as these agencies are being given preferential
treatment just because they are PSUs of the Ministry not because of their proven track
record. The Committee, thus, recommends to the Ministry to formulate set parameters for
selection of GMCs to ensure that the GMCs which actually require upgradation are selected
in consultation with State Governments. The Committee, further, recommends that the
Ministry, while appointing consultancy agencies, should also take into consideration past
reputation and good track record of the agencies in order to avoid time and cost overruns.
Accordingly, the Committee recommends for involvement of better professional agencies or
other reputed construction majors to ensure cost effective and timely execution especially

116
in projects where HSCC has failed to ensure timely completion of the construction projects.
The Committee also takes a serious note on part of the PSA in undertaking a proper gap
analysis in GMCs where requisite medical equipment were not provided on a timely basis.
Site Selection and Status of Construction Activities in GMCs
8.24 The ap proval for Phases-I, II and III of work relating to upgradation of GMCs was given
in June 2006, February 2009 and November 2013 respectively with stipulated period of completion
being three years from the date of approval for Phases-I and II and 43 months for Phase-III. Work
for Phase-I sites selected could, however, be awarded only during the period from January 2007
to April 2011. Under Phase-II and Phase-III the works were awarded during the period from
January 2011 to June 2016 and May 2016 to December 2016 respectively. As such, there were
considerable delays in planning and commencement of works in all three phases.
8.25 W ith respect to the status of the construction work, the Committee has been informed that
the upgradation has been completed in 12 out of 13 GMCs approved for upgradation in the Phases-I
and three out of six GMCs under Phase-II of PMSSY . Only one college out of 39 colleges
approved under Phase-III is completed yet and construction activities at other Institutes are still in
progress. Further, construction has been started in some GMCs under Phase-IV and V and tender
has been floated in case of other GMCs. The upgradation of 15 GMCs under Phase-IV and V A has
been approved in August, 2016 and scheduled to be completed in March, 2020.
8.26 It has also been submitted that for the Phase-III and later phases of upgradation projects,
Ministry in consultation with the State Governments has focused on augmentation of the post
graduation (PG) seats in the process of creation of the super-specialty infrastructure. Under the
gap analysis process, agreement of the State Government has also been taken for creation of the
PG seats as would become feasible with the operationalization of the new facilities. Upgradation of
GMCs undertaken in Phase-III and Phases-IV and V A are yet not complete. Status of upgradation
of GMCs under all the phases of PMSSY has been given in Annexure-D .
8.27 The CAG in its report highlighted that  as per MoU between State Governments and the
Ministry for upgradation of GMCs during Phase-III of the scheme, the State Governments had to
ensure availability of encumbrance free land for construction of the Super Specialty Blocks (SSB)
of the GMC within 30 days of approval of the DPR. However, in five instances, the State
Governments concerned failed to provide a clear site in time leading to delay in the upgradation
of these GMCs. In some GMCs, work was awarded at higher cost. In Nizam’s Institute of Medical
Sciences (NIMS), Hyderabad, tender for construction of Super specialty Block and the Accident
Trauma Hospital were awarded at a cost of ` 125.91 crore which was 22.37 per cent above the
approved cost and 12.9 per cent above the justified market rate.
8.28 The Committee during the course of its study visit observes that construction activities
at various Institutes are delayed. The reasons for delays are manifold including (i) non-
availability of encumbrance free land (ii) delays in getting clearances for excavation
(iii) tree cutting and other site related conditions (iv) changes made in the scope and
quantum of work (v) post contract changes in drawings and quantities (vi) delays in providing
drawings (vii) delay in release of mobilization advance and payments to contractor (viii)
delay in provision of services (ix) delay in work due to shortage of labour (x) delay in

117
finalisation/tendering of medical equipment (xi) changes in site after award of work delay
in shifting of existing electrical lines (xii) internal disturbances in some States etc. The
Committee urges the Ministry to flag these issues with the State Government concerned to
undertake appropriate steps to remove the bottlenecks causing delay in the completion of
construction activities at various GMCs.
8.29 The Committee, further, observes that the work of 12 GMCs out of 13 approved under
Phase-I, scheduled to be completed in March, 2013, have been completed with delays ranging
from eight months to seven years. In other six GMCs approved under Phase-II, the upgradation
of only three GMCs has been completed though with the delay of several years. In the
remaining three colleges, the work has not been completed even after many years. The
revised date of completion has been extended to 31st December, 2018 for GMCs which
initially that were scheduled to be completed in July, 2011.
8.30 The Committee takes serious note of issue of awarding of tender at the cost higher
than the approved cost indicating financial irregularities. The Committee believes that the
whole process should be objective and on merit rather than on any other consideration so
that the agency with the most economical and best offer of services is awarded the tender
for completion of the projects.
8.31 The Committee takes into account that only one GMC out of 39 GMCs of Phase-III i.e.
GMC, Kota has been completed so far. 18 GMCs that were scheduled to be completed by the year
2017 have not been completed yet and the revised date of completion has been set. Further,
13 GMCs in phase-III that were scheduled to be completed till 2018, have not been completed yet.
Out of these 13 GMCs, work of upgradation has not crossed even 70 per cent in 8 GMCs. The
work for these GMCs had commenced only during the period from May, 2016 to December, 2016.
8.32 The Committee believes that the Ministry cannot in any way justify the inordinate
delays in the completion of the projects. Procedural and preparatory exercises need to be
done beforehand including availability of encumbrance free site by the respective State
Government. The Committee also recommends to the Ministry to frame operational guidelines
that would guide and regulate implementation of the scheme across the States and take
steps to expedite the completion of remaining work by better monitoring of the projects.
The Committee apprehends that such delays will increase the work load at the fag end of
completion schedule. The Committee, therefore, is of the considered view that priority
should be given to such projects for which there is imminent need to expedite the process
of granting necessary approvals only to avoid time and cost overruns are avoided.  The
Committee also strongly recommends that no new project be taken before completion of
these 73 projects.
8.33 The Committee understands that there may be certain practical difficulties that are
encountered on work sites during the course of upgradation project. However the, considerable
delays in planning and commencement of works in all phases of upgradation of GMCs under
PMSSY and the slow progress, both at the stage of planning and contracting indicates that
both planning of works and contract management were inadequate and improper, thus causing
adverse impact in the delivery of services. The Committee is of the firm view that the

118
Ministry/Central Government, instead of taking the responsibility, has shifted the blame on
the State Governments for the delay in the commencement of upgradation of GMCs under
PMSSY. The Committee feels that instead of blame game, the Ministry should work in
tandem with the State Governments and help in ironing out problem areas so that the
objectives of the scheme is not defeated by delays and faulty planning. The Committee,
therefore, recommends to the Ministry to review the status of construction timelines and
set realistically achievable targets in consultation with the State Governments concerned.
Procurement of Equipment
8.34 The Committee has been given to understand that as per the procurement procedure policy
for medical equipment under Phase I, II and III of PMSSY , procurement of medical equipment
would be handled by designated Procurement Support Agency (PSA) i.e., HITES which is a 100%
subsidiary of HLL Life care Ltd. for Phase I, II and III of PMSSY . It was the role and responsibility
of Procurement Support Agent to:–
(i) ensure procurement of state of art, genuine, reliable medical equipment with emphasis
on ensuring protection of public interest through savings quality etc.
(ii) strict compliance of GFR/CVC guidelines.
(iii) ensure multi-vendor participation and procurement of Made in India medical equipment
wherever applicable.
(iv) provide all possible support to Ministry as and when required.
(v) link up process of procurement with construction sites.
8.35 The Committee was further informed that, although HLL has been appointed as PSA for
procurement of medical equipment for Phase-I and II, yet there have been considerable delays in
procurement mainly due to several approvals needed from the Ministry. That necessitated revision
of existing procedure and policy to simplify the process and accordingly the policy and procedure
for procurement of medical equipment was revised as enshrined below-
(i) PSA is entrusted with responsibility to prepare preliminary List of Requirement (LoR)
and draft technical specification by conducting survey and gap viability analysis and
preparing LoR for each Institution. This is done by the PSA through a Technical
Specification Committee (TSC), members of which are to drawn from AIIMS and other
Institutes of National Importance (INI). The Ministry will, then obtain the list of the
specialty-wise panel of experts from AIIMS, INIs and will make this list available to the
PSA. PSA may choose required number of experts, minimum two, from the panel given
by the Ministry for each specialty and must ensure that multi vendor and genuine
manufacturer participation is achieved in a transparent manner. Approval of specification
should be made within 45 days from the date of receipt of approved LoR and technical
Specifications from all medical colleges.
(ii) PSA is, then, responsible for getting approval of pre-bid amendments in technical specification
from  TSC  within  15 days from  the  date  of  pre-bid meeting and also for adherence
to all extant Government of India guidelines, rules instructions etc. PSA should then

119
examine and suitably dispose the representations/complaints received with this regard
within 7 days from the date of receipt of representation/complaint. After approval of
pre-bid amendments, the Technical, Commercial and Financial bid evaluation will be
done by PSA in accordance with the provisions of GFR, DFPR¸CVC and any other
financial/commercial notifications. The evaluation report will be submitted to the Ministry
for concurrence of IFD before submission to IPC. PSA should then make placement in
IPC in consultation with the Ministry within two weeks from the date of receipt of IFD
concurrence from Ministry.
(iii) Based on the decision taken in by the IPC, the Ministry shall communicate approval of
the competent authority to the PSA with concurrence of IFD for issue of Notification
of Award (NOA) and will release the necessary funds to PSA with concurrence of IFD.
PSA then, within 7 days from the date of receipt of approval, should place orders in
terms of the approval communicated. At the end, PSA will procure Consignee Receipt
Certificate (CRC) and Final Acceptance Certificate and submit to the Ministry. Time
taken from techno-commercial evaluation to placement of order should be completed
within two months.

8.38 The CAG report (2018) highlighted many discrepancies in the procurement of equipment. As
per the procurement guidelines and provisions of the MoU signed between GMCs and the Ministry,
GMCs had to ensure that no alterations and additions were made to the list of equipment and
specifications firmed up by the medical experts. In RIMS-Ranchi, JNMC-Aligarh, BMCRI-Bangalore,
IMS-Varanasi, GMC-Mumbai and GMC-Nagpur, 293 medical equipment costing ` 19.86 crore were
procured for installation in the upgraded facilities and these equipment did not fall in the approved
list of medical equipment of the Ministry. Further, as per the instructions, the equipment cost was
to include the cost of warranty and the Institutions were to enter into Comprehensive Maintenance
Contracts (CMC) at the cost of the State Government before expiry of warranty period. It was,
however, found that that the warranty period of 147 medical equipment costing ` 27.90 crore in
GMKMC-Salem, IMS-Varanasi and GMC-Amritsar had expired three months to three years ago.
However, the concerned GMCs had not entered into Comprehensive Maintenance Contract CMCs
for the equipment.
8.39 The CAG report (2018) further highlighted that due to improper gap analysis for equipment
costing ` 12.86 crore were procured/being procured from State  funds had also been included in
the list of equipment for procurement under PMSSY . Thus, there was duplication in the plan for
procurement of equipment. At the same time, requirement for various equipment of five departments
of GMC-Kota were not included in the gap analysis report. At BJMC-Ahmedabad, the Ministry
approved (February, 2009) procurement of 294 equipment at an estimated cost of ` 37.69 crore
for BJMC-Ahmedabad. Subsequently, in August, 2013, BJMC-Ahmedabad was asked to review its
equipment list as it contained items not directly connected with tertiary healthcare viz. CCTV, lift,
ramps, laundry machine, etc. The Institute submitted a revised list of equipment to the Ministry
(October, 2013) including three new equipment costing ` 9.58 crore. The three new equipment
were not accepted by the Ministry (January, 2014) on the ground that those items had not been
included in the gap analysis. Thus, the Institute could not obtain funds for equipment required by
it due to improper gap analysis.
8.40 In a specific query about instances where in the process of tendering, multiple bids were
received but due to disqualification of other bidders, tenders were left with a single eligible bid,
the Ministry submitted details of GMCs with single responsive bid. The Ministry submitted that in
several cases even through multiple bids were received for procurement of equipment, only single
bid was found techno commercially responsive and the tenders were processed as per Ministry’s
IFD guidelines.
8.41 The Committee notes with concern the observations of CAG regarding improper gap
analysis, lacunae in CMC provisions and procurement of equipment which did not fall in the
approved list of medical equipment of the Ministry. The CAG Report further highlights that
against the procurement orders for 818 equipment costing ````` 482.21 crore for 11 GMCs, 191
equipment costing ````` 51.72 crore were yet to be made available. The Committee is concerned
to note that there are several tenders which are pending since very long and are being
retendered again and again. The Committee notes that the basic purpose of having a PSA

121
stands defeated if such delays are going to occur. The Committee, in this connection,
strongly recommends for a properly monitored mechanism, so as to ensure that time and
cost overruns in the procurement process are avoided. The Committee is surprised to note
that a total of 141 tenders for the procurement of equipment are pending under Phase-III
of the upgradation project under PMSSY. The Committee observes that these 141 tenders
have been retendered by the Ministry in the year 2018. Out of these, 4 tenders for surgical
loupes, extra corporeal membrane oxygenator, head saver and surgical xenon head light and
light sources have again been floated. Also, 24 types of equipment under Phase-I and II and
7 types of equipment under Phase-III have been procured on a single bid basis. The Committee
desires the PSA to submit a status note in all the procurement carried out on single bid
basis in Phase-I and Phase-II including reasons for the same, within three months of
presentation of this report.
8.42 The Committee observes that there is an acute shortage of equipment at the various
GMCs approved for upgradation under PMSSY. The primary reasons being delays in placement
of orders, change in the model of the equipment and lack of follow up by Institutes with
the nominated PSA after placement of orders. The Committee apprehends that in the
absence of the equipment, the scheme gets affected and patients are deprived of upgraded
services. The CAG has further highlighted a grave concern i.e. 75 equipment have been
supplied by HLL at a cost of ````` 3.26 crore but are not anywhere in record either with HLL
or the concerned GMCs.  The Committee takes a serious note of this lapse and recommends
for suitable remedial action to address this criminal wastage of public fund. The Committee
would also like to be apprised of the action taken by the Ministry for fixing accountability
for this lapse.
8.43 The Committee is, therefore, of the considered view that procurement of equipment on
single bid basis reduces the competition in the market and minimizes the opportunity of
competitive bidding. The Committee would like the Ministry to adhere to the procedure of
the multiple bids in order to achieve competitive pricing.
8.44 The Committee observes that the revised policy and procedure formulated for procurement
of medical equipment has not been followed in letter and spirit. The Committee strongly
recommends that there should be minimum pendency and in the procurement process and
all pending procurement tenders be closed without any further delay. The Ministry should
also formulate effective monitoring mechanism for timely receipt, installation and proper
functioning of equipment at GMCs so that the equipment are utilized properly for the
purpose for which they were procured. A quarterly update on gap analysis, delivery of
equipment, delays if any, with respect to all GMCs should be submitted to the Committee
by the PSA.
Enhancement of PG Seats
8.45 Pertaining to the status of Post Graduate Seats and Graduate courses in GMC’s under
PMSSY , the Committee has been informed that since the GMC upgradation projects essentially
involve augmentation of the tertiary healthcare infrastructure in already existing GMCs, enhancement

122
seats. However, in the case of Phase-III and later phase upgradation projects, the attempt has been
